config.title: Conditional Classes

intro.title: Conditional Classes
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a simple notification component that changes its appearance based on different message types. You'll learn how to conditionally apply CSS classes to React elements using JavaScript expressions. The main technologies involved are React JSX, JavaScript ternary operators, and template literals for string concatenation. By the end, you'll understand how to dynamically control styling based on component state or props.
intro.usecase: Conditional classes are essential for creating dynamic, responsive interfaces that react to user interactions and application state. In real-world applications, you'll use them to highlight active navigation items in dashboards, indicate form validation errors, toggle dark/light themes, or show loading states on buttons. For example, when a user selects a filter option in an e-commerce site, conditional classes visually distinguish the active filter from inactive ones. This pattern appears everywhere from social media platforms that mark unread notifications to project management tools that indicate task completion status through visual cues.

objectives: Apply conditional logic to dynamically assign CSS classes based on component state
Construct ternary expressions to toggle between multiple class names
Implement template literals with embedded expressions for conditional class strings
Configure class binding for multiple conditional classes using logical operators
Manipulate component appearance by updating state variables that control conditional classes
Integrate conditional classes with event handlers to create interactive UI feedback
Render components with varying visual styles controlled by boolean state values

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have React and useState available to use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function. Make sure to export the component.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns an empty div.
successCriteria: The App component is created and returns an empty div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the main App component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the App component returns an empty div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component is not correctly defined or doesn't return an empty div.

steps.title: Initialize state for toggle
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'isActive' with an initial value of false.
steps.hint: Call useState(false) and destructure the returned array into isActive and setIsActive.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a boolean state variable
const [isOn, setIsOn] = useState(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'isActive' initialized to false, ready to control conditional styling.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with false, and the returned array is destructured into isActive and setIsActive.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with false and destructuring both isActive and setIsActive from the returned array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the App component, use useState(false) to create a state variable named isActive.

steps.title: Define toggle handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named 'handleToggle' that toggles the isActive state between true and false.
steps.hint: You can use the setter function from useState to update the state. For toggling, you can pass a function to setState that receives the previous value and returns its opposite.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleToggle function that toggles the isActive state value when called.
successCriteria: The handleToggle function is defined inside the App component and correctly toggles the isActive state using setIsActive.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function uses setIsActive to toggle the boolean value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't toggle the state correctly. Check that you're using setIsActive with the previous state value.

steps.title: Add a button to toggle state
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add a button element with the text 'Toggle Style' and wire its onClick event to the handleToggle function.
steps.hint: Add the button JSX element inside the existing div. Remember to use the onClick attribute and pass the handleToggle function reference.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with an event handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button with 'Toggle Style' text appears in the UI that will toggle the isActive state when clicked.
successCriteria: The button element is added with text 'Toggle Style' and has onClick={handleToggle}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but check that it has the exact text 'Toggle Style' and the onClick handler is properly wired to handleToggle.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't correctly implemented. Make sure you're adding a button element with the specified text and onClick handler inside the div.

steps.title: Create a div with conditional class
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a div element with a className that conditionally includes 'active' when isActive is true and 'inactive' when false.
steps.hint: Use a ternary operator to set the className based on the isActive state value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A div element with conditional CSS classes that change based on the isActive state.
successCriteria: The div element has a className attribute using a ternary operator that sets 'active' when isActive is true and 'inactive' when false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a div, but check that the className uses a ternary operator with isActive to switch between 'active' and 'inactive'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The div element is missing or the className isn't conditionally set based on isActive. Try using className={isActive ? 'active' : 'inactive'}.

steps.title: Display current state value
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element that displays the current value of the isActive state.
steps.hint:
Use JSX interpolation to show the isActive variable inside a

tag.
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph showing the current boolean value of isActive appears below the button.
successCriteria: A paragraph element displays the current value of isActive using JSX interpolation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're showing the isActive variable inside a paragraph element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element isn't displaying the isActive state value correctly.

steps.title: Add text content to styled div
steps.instruction: Inside the conditionally styled div, add text content that describes its current state.
steps.hint: You can add a simple text string or a template literal that references the isActive state.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding content to a styled element
This item is {isHighlighted ? 'highlighted' : 'normal'}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The conditionally styled div now contains descriptive text that changes based on the isActive state.
successCriteria: The conditionally styled div contains text content that references or describes the current state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added content to the div, but make sure it clearly reflects the current state (like mentioning 'active' or 'inactive').
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditionally styled div still lacks text content. Add some text inside the div to describe its state.

steps.title: Test the conditional class behavior
steps.instruction: Click the toggle button in your preview and observe how the div's class and appearance change between 'active' and 'inactive' states.
steps.hint: The button toggles the isActive state, which changes the className on the div from 'inactive' to 'active' and vice versa.
steps.analogousExample:
// Testing interactive behavior
// Click the button and watch the element's style change
steps.expectedOutcome: When you click the Toggle button, the div should visually change between the active and inactive styles.
successCriteria: The toggle button works and the div's class switches between 'active' and 'inactive' based on the isActive state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: The toggle button might not be working correctly. Make sure the onClick handler is properly set to handleToggle and the className ternary uses isActive.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional class behavior isn't working. Check that your button has onClick={handleToggle} and the div's className uses isActive ? 'active' : 'inactive'.
